questions.prompt: What is the test for whether threat intelligence is operational?
options: Whether it comes from a paid feed
What happens differently today because it arrived -- an indicator in a PDF is not operational; the same indicator in an EDR list or blocklist is
Whether it is formatted in STIX
questions.explanation: Intelligence that does not change a detection or blocking control has not been operationalized regardless of its quality or source.

questions.prompt: Why must a new indicator trigger a retrospective search rather than only forward matching?
options: The most valuable question a new indicator answers is usually 'were we already hit?' -- and only a backward search over historical telemetry answers it
Retrospective searches are cheaper to run
Forward matching requires a SIEM license
questions.explanation: An indicator that begins matching only from today misses the compromise that already happened, which is frequently the reason the indicator was published.

questions.prompt: Why does an indicator aging policy matter?
options: IP addresses get reassigned, so old indicators generate false positives against innocent third-party infrastructure and erode trust in every alert the source produces
questions.explanation: Without decay, an intel program slowly accumulates false positives and trains analysts to disregard its alerts.

questions.prompt: Why is tactical-only intelligence consumption a weakness?
options: It is the least durable level -- hashes and IPs sit at the bottom of the Pyramid of Pain and are discarded by adversaries without effort
It requires more analyst time than operational intelligence
questions.explanation: Operational intelligence about TTPs produces detections that survive adversary changes; tactical indicators produce detections that expire quickly.
